title: Which Is More Rail
context: Grade 4, and this is the topic where the printed pages promise more than they give. An adult sees two comparison rules. What is actually being taught is which pairs each rule reaches and which pairs neither reaches. The chapter's own headings promise a general method for unlike fractions and then deliver the shared-numerator case, so a child who trusts the heading will apply a rule where it does not hold. The rail refuses that move and gives the refusal somewhere to go.

writeup.why: Find out which pairs of fractions each of this chapter's two rules can settle, and what to do with a pair that neither one reaches.
writeup.look: A rail running across the stage with two named gates on it, a parking bay at its end and a line-up board underneath.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Which Is More Rail' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the pairs settled against the pairs this phase loads, two numbers in ink, and beside them, on its own and never underneath as though it were a shortfall, the count of pairs standing in the bay. Neither count ever goes down and neither of them ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The rail runs left to right across the upper half of the working area, 1086 by 10 at 64,330, with a loading head at its left 240 by 200 at 64,230 and the two gates standing on it. The first gate is 200 by 240 at 420,210 and carries a printed label naming it for a shared lower number; the second is 200 by 240 at 700,210 and carries a printed label naming it for a shared upper number. Each label is a sentence about what that gate tests and never about which number is bigger. A gate opens only when its own test passes: inside the first, both fractions are drawn as strips of equal length cut the same number of times, and the fuller strip lifts clear in vermilion; inside the second, the two strips are cut differently and filled with the same number of parts, and the strip cut into fewer parts is drawn plainly reaching further. A gate that refuses lights the two numbers it would have compared on both fractions, writes nothing, marks nothing and lets the pair roll on. The parking bay is 240 by 240 at 980,210, drawn in sky blue with a printed label standing over it, and it is a settled end state rather than an error: a pair that both gates refused rolls in, comes to rest, and the bay prints beside it that this pair shares neither number and that no rule in this chapter reaches it. Nothing in the bay is ever red, nothing in it is ever crossed through, and nothing ever pushes a parked pair back out onto the rail by itself. The line-up board runs 1086 by 190 at 64,530, three to six card slots along it with the direction switch 200 by 48 at its right reading ascending or descending; a slot takes a card only once the whole set has been checked for what its members share, and a small strip is drawn under each card so the finished order can be read off the pictures as well as off the numbers. The whole number reader sits at 64,470, 240 by 48, and draws any fraction written over one as that many complete whole circles in green. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across where a number is asked for, with three comparison keys beside them reading is greater than, is less than, and cannot be settled yet. The third key is the same size and the same weight as the other two, because on this rail it is an answer and not a way out of answering. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the parts a fraction counts are deep blue, the parts of that same whole which it leaves are amber, a whole shown entire or a bracket spanning one whole is green, a second writing of an amount already on the stage is rose, the greater of two fractions one of the chapter's rules can settle is vermilion, and a pair neither rule settles is sky blue, which is how this stage says undecided without saying wrong. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told from the rest by the drawn cut between them and by the label under it before it is ever told by a fill, and every cut, score line, cell edge and guide line is near-black. A fraction is drawn everywhere with its upper number above a level horizontal line and its lower number below, both upright and centred, and a mixed number is drawn as an upright whole number standing beside a stacked fraction. The bay is never drawn as a bin, a cross, a question mark or an empty box. It is a labelled place with a printed reason standing over it, and a pair in it has been correctly handled. A child who reaches it has read both gates and found that neither one tests anything these two fractions have in common, which is a piece of work and not a failure to do one.
writeup.finish: The card shows every pair the child sent down the rail, which gate took each one, and anything standing in the not yet bay still labelled with the reason it is there.

phases.win: the gate opens, the strips are drawn with the same cuts, and the fuller one is lifted out
phases.does: sends the pair through the first gate and reads the two strips inside it
phases.goal: like fractions are compared by their upper numbers
phases.says: These two are cut the same way. So what is left to compare?
phases.check: Put the right sign between 3/10 and 8/10, and tell me which pair of numbers you used to decide.
phases.feels: the pieces are the same size on both strips, so there is only one thing left that can separate them
phases.hands: Cut two identical paper strips, fold both into elevenths, and colour seven parts of one and four of the other. Lay them one under the other from a ruled margin and ask what is the same about the two pictures before asking which is more.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: are the two numbers below the lines the same? Second rung, the phase's: so what is left that can be different? Third rung: the gate is opened with both strips drawn and cut but neither filled, and the child fills each from its own upper number. The comparison keys stay open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the lower number has done the deciding on every question since the chapter began, so it is the number the eye goes to first.
wrong.move: compares the two lower numbers, which are identical and cannot decide anything.
wrong.screen: the gate opens and draws both strips cut the same number of times, with the eleven cuts counted out along each and printed as equal. The two lower numbers are then lit together and read out as the same number, so nothing about them separates the pair, and the two upper numbers light next with the filled parts counted along each strip. The child's answer stays in the slot and both strips stay drawn.

wrong.why: a fraction still looks like two ordinary numbers, and adding them turns each one into a single number that can be compared the ordinary way.
wrong.move: adds the two numbers of each fraction together and compares the totals.
wrong.screen: the child's two totals are printed where they were worked out and are not crossed through, because on this pair they happen to agree with the strips. The rail then loads three quarters against three eighths and runs the same move on it: the totals come to seven and eleven, so the move picks three eighths, and the second gate is opened on the same pair with both strips cut and filled, where three quarters plainly reaches further. Both runs are left standing together.

phases.screen: a pair whose lower numbers match waiting at the head of the rail
phases.soWhat: When two fractions share a lower number they are like fractions, the pieces are the same size, and the one with the larger upper number is the larger fraction.

phases.win: the second gate opens and the strip cut into fewer parts is shown reaching further
phases.does: sends the pair on to the second gate and compares the two strips
phases.goal: fractions sharing an upper number are compared by their lower numbers
phases.says: You are taking the same number of pieces each time. Which pieces are bigger?
phases.check: Which is greater, 7/8 or 7/20, and would your reason still work if both top numbers were one instead of seven?
phases.feels: the same number of pieces taken both times, so the only thing left to decide it is how big a piece is
phases.hands: Fold one strip into quarters and an identical strip into eighths, and colour three parts of each. Lay them from a ruled margin and ask which reaches further, then ask how many pieces were coloured on each one. Do it again with fifths against twelfths, five parts coloured on both.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: are the two numbers above the lines the same? Second rung, the phase's: which of the two wholes was cut into fewer pieces? Third rung: the gate is opened with one part of each strip lifted out and laid side by side, so the piece sizes are compared before any counting. The comparison keys stay open.

wrong.why: a larger number has meant a larger amount everywhere else in arithmetic, and nothing about a fraction announces that the lower number works the other way round.
wrong.move: picks the fraction with the larger lower number, choosing 5/12 over 5/6 because twelve is more than six.
wrong.screen: the gate opens and cuts both strips from the same left edge, one into six parts and one into twelve, with a single part of each lifted out and laid side by side so the difference in piece size is the thing on the stage. Five parts are then filled on each strip, one at a time and in step, and the run of five bigger pieces stops further along. The child's choice stays in the slot and both strips stay drawn.

wrong.why: the rule has been met as a rule about unit fractions, so a pair with a shared upper number of three looks like a pair the gate was not built for.
wrong.move: refuses the pair 3/4 against 3/8 at the second gate because neither of its upper numbers is one, and sends it on to the bay.
wrong.screen: the bay hands the pair straight back and prints why, because the bay takes only pairs that share neither number and this pair shares its upper number. The second gate's label is read out as it is printed, a sentence about a shared upper number with no mention of what that number has to be, and the gate then opens on the pair and cuts both strips, three parts filled on each. The child's send is left drawn as a faint line along the rail.

phases.screen: a pair whose upper numbers match, refused by the first gate
phases.soWhat: For any pair that share a numerator, the smaller denominator gives the larger fraction, because cutting a whole into fewer parts makes every part bigger.
phases.concept: Same count, so size the pieces

phases.win: the cards settle in order, the direction label is read aloud and the strips beside them grow the same way
phases.does: finds what the whole set shares, then slides the cards into order
phases.goal: a set is ordered by whatever its members share
phases.says: What do all of these have in common? Order them by whatever is left.
phases.check: Arrange 6/5, 6/11, 6/7 and 6/2 in ascending order, and say what the set shares.
phases.feels: one list has its bottom numbers running downwards while the fractions themselves run up
phases.hands: Peg a card marked nothing at one end of a string and a card marked one whole at the other, and hand out a set of cards that all share a lower number. Have them pegged up, then take them down and hand out a set that all share an upper number instead, and ask what changed about the way the set had to be read.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what do all four of these cards have in common? Second rung, the phase's: which rule compares that kind of pair? Third rung: the board is cut to two cards from the set, ordered as a pair before the other two come back. Nothing placed on the board is ever marked wrong.

wrong.why: the lower number has been the important one for most of the chapter, so it is the column the eye runs down first.
wrong.move: orders a set of like fractions by their lower numbers, which are all identical and carry no information at all.
wrong.screen: the four cards are laid in a row with their lower numbers lit together and read out as one number repeated four times, and the board will not accept an order built on them. The upper numbers light next and a small strip is drawn under each card, filled from its own fraction, so the four strips grow in the same direction as the four upper numbers. The child's arrangement stays on the board while the strips are drawn beneath it.

wrong.why: ascending means going up, the numbers being sorted are the lower ones, and putting numbers in increasing order is the move that phrase has always meant.
wrong.move: puts a shared-numerator set in order by writing its lower numbers out in increasing order, and hands in the reverse of what was asked.
wrong.screen: a strip is drawn under every card, all of one length, each cut into its own lower number and filled with six parts, and the four strips are stood in the order the child chose. The fills plainly shorten from left to right while the direction switch reads ascending, and the switch is lit rather than moved. The child's order stays on the board and the strips stay drawn beneath it.

phases.screen: four fractions on the line-up board with the direction set to ascending
phases.soWhat: Find what the whole set shares before deciding anything, because that is what says which of the two rules orders it.

phases.win: the pair parks in the not yet bay with the reason printed beside it and nothing guessed
phases.does: tries each gate, sees both refuse, and sends the pair to the bay
phases.goal: a pair sharing neither number cannot be settled by this chapter
phases.says: Neither gate will take this pair. What can you honestly say about it?
phases.check: Which is greater, 4/5 or 7/9? Say which gate would take that pair, and what your answer is.
phases.feels: both gates look at this pair and neither of them is asking about anything the two fractions have
phases.hands: Hand out a pair that shares neither of its numbers, such as three sevenths against five eighths, and ask which rule would settle it. Let the class try both and find that neither one asks about anything this pair has. Then ask what they would need to be given in order to place it, and write that down as the thing still to come rather than as a failure.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: do the two numbers below the lines match? Second rung, the phase's: do the two numbers above the lines match? Third rung: the rail is cut to the two gates alone with their labels read out one after the other, so what each one tests is heard before the pair is pushed. Parking the pair is one of the three answer keys and none of the rungs ever pushes towards a guess.

wrong.why: the rule about a smaller lower number was the last one taught and it is the one nearest to hand, and nothing about this pair announces that it is out of that rule's reach.
wrong.move: settles the pair anyway on its lower numbers, picking 3/7 over 5/8 because seven is the smaller of the two.
wrong.screen: the pair is sent back to the head of the rail and each gate says again what it tests, with the two numbers it would have compared lit on both fractions: the lower numbers are seven and eight and do not match, the upper numbers are three and five and do not match either. Neither gate opens and no strips are drawn, because there is no rule here to draw them for. The pair rolls on into the bay with its reason printed, and the child's verdict stays in the slot beside it, unmarked.

wrong.why: the bay has just been met and it is the easiest place on the rail to send something to, and a pair with a one underneath it looks like nothing the rules were about.
wrong.move: sends a pair that one of the two gates does take to the bay, because the numbers look unfamiliar.
wrong.screen: the bay hands the pair back and prints the test it failed to fail: it takes only pairs that share neither number, and 9/1 against 9/4 shares its upper number. The second gate then opens on the pair, cuts both strips and fills nine parts on each, and the whole number reader draws the one written underneath as nine complete circles in green. The child's send is left drawn as a faint line along the rail and nothing is marked.

phases.screen: a pair sharing no number at all rolling past both gates
phases.soWhat: A pair sharing neither of its numbers cannot be settled by either rule in this chapter, and saying so is the correct answer rather than a gap.
phases.concept: Pairs these two rules cannot settle

writeup.delight: The second gate, the moment it opens on three quarters against three eighths. The two strips do not appear side by side already filled. They are cut while a hand watches, the upper one into four parts and the lower one into eight, from the same left edge and to the same length, and then three parts are filled on each, one at a time and in step, so the same count is plainly being taken both times. The two fills stop in different places, and a measuring line drops from the longer one down to the shorter to say how much further. Neither shared upper number is one, which is the point of running it on this pair: the gate is not a rule about halves and quarters and thirds, it is a rule about taking the same number of pieces out of wholes that were cut differently. Nothing else on the rail moves and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase two written fractions sit at the head of the rail with their lower numbers plainly matching, both gates shut ahead of them and the bay at the far end empty. On the second a pair whose upper numbers match stands just past the first gate, which has already let it through untouched, with the second gate shut in front of it. On the third four fraction cards lie on the line-up board below the rail, out of order, with the direction switch reading ascending and every slot empty. On the fourth a pair sharing neither of its numbers waits at the head of the rail, both gates shut, and the bay at the end is drawn open in the undecided colour with its label already printed and nothing standing in it. The running count at the top left holds the pairs settled against the pairs this phase loads, with the pairs parked counted beside them rather than under them. One thing moves, once: the two lower numbers, or the two upper numbers, or the shortest card on the board, or the empty bay, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what this pair has in common. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any pair or set of fractions on the rail, both gates live, the not yet bay open and the line-up board set ascending or descending. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on comparing like fractions, comparing fractions sharing an upper number, ordering a set either way, and saying when a pair cannot be settled yet.
voiceLines: A pair at the head of the rail. Before you push, say what these two fractions share.
These two are cut the same way. So what is left to compare?
You are taking the same number of pieces each time. Which pieces are bigger?
What do all of these have in common? Order them by whatever is left.
Neither gate will take this pair. What can you honestly say about it?
Another pair. Look at the bottom numbers first, then the top ones.
Free play. Any pair or any set on the rail, both gates live and the bay open.
Send it back and read each gate's label out. Every gate says what it tests.
Every pair sent where it belongs, and the ones neither gate reaches still parked and still labelled.

observations.why: One gate tests whether the pieces are the same size and the other tests whether the same count of pieces is being taken.
observations.soWhat: Learn the two rules by what they compare, because learnt as rules about big and small numbers they get swapped inside a week.
observations.observe: Each gate said what it tested before it would open, and neither label mentioned a bigger or a smaller number.

observations.why: Cutting a whole into fewer parts makes every part bigger, and taking the same count of bigger parts reaches further.
observations.soWhat: For any pair that share a numerator, the smaller denominator gives the larger fraction, whatever that shared upper number happens to be.
observations.observe: Inside the second gate the strip cut into fewer parts reached further, and it did that whether the shared upper number was one or three.

observations.why: The set shared a numerator, so the fraction with the largest lower number is the smallest of them.
observations.soWhat: Find what the whole set shares first, because the rule decides the direction and not the other way about.
observations.observe: In one ascending list the denominators came out running downwards.

observations.why: The two rules in this chapter each need a shared number, and those pairs had neither.
observations.soWhat: When neither rule reaches a pair, saying so is the answer, and the method that would reach it has not been met yet.
observations.observe: Some pairs rolled past both gates and came to rest in the bay with a reason printed beside them.

source_tool.description: A rail runs left to right across the stage with two gates on it and a bay at the end. The first gate is labelled for a shared lower number and opens only for a pair whose lower numbers match; inside it the two fractions are drawn as strips cut the same way, and the one with more parts filled is lifted out as the larger. The second gate is labelled for a shared upper number and opens only for a pair whose upper numbers match; inside it the two strips are cut differently but filled with the same number of parts, and the strip cut into fewer parts reaches further. Each gate names what it tests, so neither is remembered as a rule about big and small numbers. The bay at the end is the not yet bay, and it is not a failure state: a pair that shares neither number is refused by both gates, rolls on, and parks there under a label saying that this chapter has no rule that reaches it. A line-up board below the rail takes three or more fractions at once and orders them by whichever gate they all pass, with an ascending and a descending setting, and a whole number reader handles a fraction written over one by drawing it as that many complete wholes.
source_tool.art_direction: A rail with two named gates and a parking bay / Picture book

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: bars and circles that are cut, paper strips laid from a common left edge, bowls that fill, trays with printed labels, loose parts that slide, and a rail with named gates along it.
A part is never drawn without its whole. Wherever a fraction is shown, the whole it came from stays in the same frame, entire, with the parts nobody took still drawn and still countable.

Every division into parts is made by a drawn cut, a score line or a gap, never by a change of colour alone. The cuts go in before any fill does, so the lower number can be counted whether anything is coloured or not.

Where a fraction says its parts are equal, every part of that whole is drawn the same size and the same shape. Where a stage deliberately shows unequal pieces, it says so in its own label and no fraction name is written against them.

A fraction is always written with its upper number above a level horizontal line and its lower number below it, both upright and centred. The line is never slanted and the two numbers are never set side by side. A mixed number is drawn as an upright whole number beside a stacked fraction.

Two fractions shown to be the same amount are drawn as strips of identical length and width, laid one directly under the other from one common left edge, so that the filled parts ending in the same place is what carries the claim.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most twenty things, separated, large enough to count at a glance and never overlapping.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a part, a strip or a token the child is counting, and a content colour is never used for chrome. The parts a fraction counts are deep blue, the parts of that same whole which it leaves are amber, and a whole shown entire or a bracket spanning one whole is green, and those three are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. A second writing of an amount already on the stage is rose, so an equivalent fraction is told from the fraction it came from without either being called wrong. The greater of two fractions one of the two rules can settle is vermilion, and a pair that neither rule settles is sky blue, which is how the stage says undecided without saying wrong. All of that holds in greyscale, because a part is told from the rest by the cut line between them and by its label before it is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.

placement.where: After fraction cards have been pegged along a string by hand and two children have disagreed about one of them. The tool is what makes each gate say what it tests before it opens, and gives an undecided pair a place to stand.

answer_key.rule: Two rules, and only two. When two fractions have the same lower number they are like fractions, the parts are the same size, and the one with the larger upper number is the larger fraction. When two fractions share an upper number the same count of parts is being taken either way, so the one cut into fewer parts wins: for any pair that share a numerator, the smaller denominator gives the larger fraction, whether or not the shared upper number happens to be one. A fraction written over one is simply the whole number above the line. To order a set, first find what the whole set shares, then use the matching rule. If a pair shares neither of its numbers, neither rule reaches it and the correct answer is that it cannot be settled with what this chapter teaches. A later method rewrites such a pair over a common denominator, and that method is not taught anywhere in these pages, so the pair parks in the not yet bay and is left there.
answer_key.wrong: The pair is sent back to the head of the rail and each gate says again what it tests, with the two numbers it compares lit on both fractions. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Both fractions are written in elevenths, so the parts are the same size in both.
When the parts are the same size, the fraction with more of them is the larger one.
Seven is more than four, so 7/11 is greater than 4/11.
items.answer: 7/11 is the greater, and the gate for a shared lower number settles it
items.question: Compare 7/11 and 4/11, and say which gate settles it.
items.checkpoint: Like fractions are compared by their upper numbers alone.
items.misconception: Comparing the lower numbers, which are the same and decide nothing here.

steps: Both fractions take five parts, so the count is the same and cannot decide it.
A whole cut into six parts gives bigger parts than the same whole cut into twelve.
Five bigger parts reach further than five smaller ones, so 5/6 is greater than 5/12.
items.question: Compare 5/6 and 5/12.
items.checkpoint: For any pair that share a numerator, the smaller denominator gives the larger fraction.
items.misconception: Choosing 5/12 because twelve is the larger number.

steps: Every fraction in the set is written in thirteenths, so they are all like fractions.
Like fractions are ordered by their upper numbers, and two is less than six, which is less than nine, which is less than eleven.
Ascending means smallest first, so the order is 2/13, 6/13, 9/13, 11/13.
items.question: Arrange 6/13, 2/13, 11/13 and 9/13 in ascending order.
items.checkpoint: Find what the whole set shares before deciding which rule to use.
items.misconception: Ordering by the lower numbers, which are identical and carry no information.

steps: The lower numbers are seven and eight, which do not match, so the first gate will not open.
The upper numbers are three and five, which do not match either, so the second gate will not open.
The pair shares no number at all, and this chapter teaches no rule for that, so the honest answer is that it needs a method not met yet.
items.answer: Neither rule reaches this pair, so it cannot be settled yet
items.question: Compare 3/7 and 5/8 using the rules of this chapter.
items.checkpoint: Saying that a pair cannot be settled yet is a correct answer, not a gap.
items.misconception: Guessing from the lower numbers alone, as though the shared-numerator rule applied here.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Put the right sign between 3/10 and 8/10.
Which is greater, 2/3 or 2/9?
items.final_answer: 2/3, because thirds are bigger parts than ninths and the same number of them is taken

items.question: Which is greater, 4/5 or 7/9, and which rule settles it?
items.final_answer: Neither rule settles it, because the pair shares no number, so it cannot be decided with what this chapter teaches

items.question: A list reads 8/6, 8/1, 8/12 and 8/3. Put it in descending order and say what 8/1 is worth.
items.final_answer: 8/1, 8/3, 8/6, 8/12, and 8/1 is worth eight whole ones

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: puts two written fractions at the head of the rail
opens for a pair whose lower numbers match and compares their upper numbers
opens for a pair whose upper numbers match and compares their lower numbers
parks a pair that neither gate takes, with the reason printed beside it
draws both fractions as strips inside whichever gate opened
orders three or more fractions, ascending or descending
draws a fraction written over one as that many complete wholes

teaching_notes: Peg fraction cards along a string by hand first, with nothing at one end and one whole at the other, and wait for two children to disagree. Then open the tool and make each gate say what it tests before it opens. The gates are named for what they compare, not for which number is bigger, because a class that learns them as rules about big and small numbers will apply the wrong one within a week. Say the shared-numerator rule for any pair that share a numerator rather than for unit fractions alone, and prove it on a pair where neither upper number is one, because the narrower version does not cover the chapter's own worked comparison. Then spend real time on the bay. Hand out a pair that shares nothing, let both gates refuse it, and accept the answer that it cannot be settled yet. There is a later method that rewrites both fractions over a common denominator, and it is not in this chapter at all, so do not reach for it and do not let a confident child reach for it either: a wrong rule applied fast is harder to undo than an honest pause. Finish on the fraction written over one, which the printed exercises set without preparing, and read it with the whole number reader as that many complete wholes.
generation_prompt: Build a fraction comparing tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A rail runs left to right across the working area with two gates standing on it and a parking bay at its right end. Two written fractions load at the head of the rail and are pushed along it. The first gate carries a printed label naming it as the gate for a shared lower number; it opens only when the two lower numbers match, and inside it both fractions are drawn as strips of equal length cut the same number of times, with the fuller strip lifting clear as the larger. The second gate carries a printed label naming it as the gate for a shared upper number; it opens only when the two upper numbers match, and inside it the two strips are cut differently but filled with the same number of parts, with the strip cut into fewer parts visibly reaching further. A gate that refuses a pair lights the two numbers it would have compared and lets the pair roll on. The parking bay at the end accepts any pair both gates refused and prints beside it that this pair shares neither number and that no rule in this chapter reaches it; the bay is drawn in the undecided colour and is a settled end state, never an error. Under the rail sits a line-up board that takes three to six fraction cards, a direction switch reading ascending or descending, and slots that accept a card only once the whole set has been checked for what it shares, with a small strip drawn under each card so the order can be read off the pictures. A whole number reader draws any fraction written over one as that many complete whole circles. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Look at the pair and say what the two fractions share. If they share the bottom number, use the first gate. If they share the top number, use the second. If they share neither, send the pair to the bay. Parking a pair there is a real answer, not a miss.
